659.title: the fire
659.hook: Sita answers, and walks into the fire
659.howItsDone: The agni-parīkṣā, Sita's trial by fire, is retold and debated in Hindu homes, temples, classrooms and women's songs; different Ramayanas tell it differently, and many tellers dwell on Sita's own words.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fire began with words: not for you, but for my honor. Rama spoke coldly to Sita in front of everyone, and she wept. Today, her answer.
screen: `NOT FOR YOU, BUT FOR MY HONOR.`

segments.voice: Sita wipes her tears. The crowd is silent: monkeys, bears, rakshasas, Lakshmana, Sugriva, Vibhishana, all waiting. And when she speaks, in Valmiki, her voice is steady. She doesn't beg. She doesn't apologize. She asks her husband a question: why are you talking to me the way a common man talks to a common woman? Then, point by point, in front of the same crowd that heard him, she answers everything he said.
screen: `SHE WIPES HER TEARS.` → `SHE DOESN'T BEG.` → `POINT BY POINT.`

segments.voice: What was in my power, she says, my heart, was always yours. When I was seized, my body was not in my power. Whose fault is that? And if you meant to give me up, why didn't you tell Hanuman when he found me? I would have let go of my life then, and spared you a war. Then she asks Lakshmana to build a fire. He looks at his brother, angry and pained, and Rama gives a sign. Lakshmana builds it. Sita walks around Rama in a circle of respect, folds her hands and calls on Agni, the god of fire, the witness of every vow: if my heart has never turned from Rama, protect me. And she walks into the flames. The crowd cries out. Then, Valmiki says, the gods come down: Brahma, Shiva, Indra and others, and Brahma tells Rama who he really is, Vishnu himself. Agni rises out of the fire holding Sita, unharmed, her clothes and garlands untouched, and declares her pure. Rama answers that he never doubted her, but the world had to see it. Hindus read this scene in many ways. In some later tellings, like the Adhyatma Ramayana and Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, the real Sita was kept safe inside the fire all along, and only a shadow was taken to Lanka; the fire simply gives her back. Others hold to Valmiki's version, and honor Sita's courage in it. And many readers today linger longest on her answer. Valmiki gave her those words. They're still there.
screen: `MY HEART WAS ALWAYS YOURS.` · `LAKSHMANA BUILDS THE FIRE.` · `AGNI GIVES HER BACK.` · `A SHADOW SITA, IN LATER TELLINGS.` · then, large: `VALMIKI GAVE HER THOSE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Sit with a straight, easy back and name to yourself something that is truly yours, that nobody can take: a value, a love, a promise you've kept. Breathe in and feel how steady it is; breathe out, and let what others have said about you fall away, just for now.
The fire. Sita answers Rama point by point, walks into the flames calling Agni to witness, and Agni himself gives her back, unharmed.
Your line: Agni gives her back. Tomorrow, the long way home begins. See you then.

660.title: the pushpaka's flight home
660.hook: a father's visit, a boon for the fallen, and a flying chariot pointed north
660.carry: the war, seen from the sky
660.howItsDone: In North India especially, Diwali remembers Rama's return to Ayodhya, and the Pushpaka's flight is often retold in the days around the festival as the journey home.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the fire. Sita answered point by point, walked into the flames, and Agni gave her back. Today, two gifts, and the flight home.

Before they leave Lanka, someone comes that Rama never expected to see again. His father. King Dasharatha, who died of grief after sending his son into exile, appears in the sky in a shining chariot. He holds Rama close for a long time, embraces Lakshmana too, and speaks kindly to Sita. And Rama, with his father in front of him at last, asks for one thing. Not for himself.

Long ago, in his grief, Dasharatha disowned Kaikeyi, who had demanded Rama's exile, and her son Bharata with her. Now Rama asks: take those words back. Be gracious to Kaikeyi and to Bharata. Dasharatha agrees. Fourteen years after the boons that broke the family, the son who was sent away asks for its healing. Then Indra offers a gift, and Rama's request is just as unexpected. Bring back the monkeys and bears who died for me, he says. Let them see their families again. Indra grants it, and the fallen get up, whole again. Now it's time to go. The fourteen years are nearly over, and Rama remembers what Bharata swore: if Rama didn't come back when the exile ended, he'd walk into a fire. There's no time to walk. So Vibhishana brings out the Pushpaka, the flying chariot that once belonged to Kubera, god of wealth, until Ravana took it. It's huge, golden, shaped like a palace, and it moves wherever its rider wishes. Rama invites everyone aboard: Sugriva, Vibhishana, the whole army. And as it rises, Rama does something tender. He shows Sita the places below. Look, there's where Ravana fell. There's where Kumbhakarna lay. There's the bridge Nala built, still crossing the sea. The war, seen from the sky, becomes a story told to the person it was for.

segments.voice: Imagine rising slowly above your last few months, like the Pushpaka lifting off, and look down at one place where something hard happened and one place where help came. Don't analyze; just point them out to yourself, the way Rama showed Sita, and breathe.

661.title: the pushpaka's flight home
661.hook: fourteen years of exile seen backward from the sky, and Hanuman sent ahead to watch Bharata's face
661.howItsDone: In the days before Diwali, Hindu families often clean and decorate their homes for a festival that, in North India especially, remembers Rama's return to Ayodhya; Bharata's welcome is often part of the retelling.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Pushpaka, the flying chariot, and the war seen from the sky, after Rama asked forgiveness for Kaikeyi and Bharata, and life for the fallen. Today, the long road home, in reverse.

Over Kishkindha, Sita asks Rama for something. She wants the wives of the monkey leaders, Tara and the others, to come with them to Ayodhya and share the homecoming. So the Pushpaka comes down, and the women climb aboard in their best clothes. Rama agrees at once. The woman who spent months among strangers wants to arrive home surrounded by friends.

Then the flight north becomes the whole story, told backward. Rama points out the places one by one. There's Rishyamuka, where I met Sugriva. There's Lake Pampa, where I grieved for you. There's Panchavati, where Ravana took you. There's Chitrakuta, where Bharata came to find me. There's the Ganga. They land at the sage Bharadvaja's hermitage on the very day the fourteen years are complete, and Rama makes a careful decision. He doesn't fly straight into Ayodhya. He sends Hanuman ahead, first to Guha, his old friend at the river crossing, and then to Bharata, with a strange instruction. Tell him I'm coming, and watch his face. If, after fourteen years of ruling, he wants to keep the kingdom, let him have it. Some readers hear a test in it. Others hear respect: Rama won't take back the throne from a brother who might have grown into it. Hanuman finds Bharata at Nandigram, outside the capital, living like a hermit, in bark clothes and matted hair, with Rama's sandals on the throne, ruling in his name. Rama is coming, Hanuman tells him. Bharata falls to the ground with joy, then gets up and embraces him. His face answers Rama's question before he says a word. And that news sets the whole city getting ready.
screen: `THE EXILE UNROLLS BACKWARD.` · `BHARADVAJA'S HERMITAGE.` · `WATCH BHARATA'S FACE.` · `RAMA'S SANDALS ON THE THRONE.` · then, large: `HIS FACE ANSWERS FOR HIM.`

662.title: Diwali
662.howItsDone: Ramayana reciters often read the homecoming and the meeting with Bharata as their own episode, and in much of North India families tell Rama's return as the reason Diwali lamps are lit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, paduka: Rama's sandals on the throne, and Hanuman sent ahead to watch Bharata's face. Your line was the road, seen from above. Today, the chariot comes down.

Why are the lamps lit at Diwali? One answer you'll hear from people who grew up with the festival: because Rama came home, and the whole city lit lamps so he could find his way. It's a lovely picture. So here's a surprise. Open Valmiki's Ramayana to the homecoming and look for the lamps. Valmiki describes flags, flowers, music, roads sprinkled with water, a crowd so big it fills the streets. A city lit by rows of lamps isn't the picture he paints. The lamps seem to have arrived later, as the story moved into the festival. Today, what Valmiki does tell: the homecoming itself, and the man at the center of it, who isn't Rama.
screen: `WHY THE LAMPS?` → `BECAUSE RAMA CAME HOME.` → `WHAT VALMIKI ACTUALLY SAYS.`

segments.voice: Bharata never wanted the throne. For fourteen years he has lived outside Ayodhya, in a village called Nandigram, in bark clothing, with matted hair, ruling only as a caretaker, with Rama's sandals set on the throne. Now Valmiki turns to what Bharata does with the news, and his joy is the center of the chapter. He orders the roads leveled and watered, the city decorated, the musicians out. Then the pushpaka comes into sight, and Bharata goes out to meet it on foot, carrying the sandals. When Rama steps down, Bharata bows, and then does the thing he's waited fourteen years to do. He puts the sandals back on his brother's feet. The kingdom, he says, was a deposit left with me; I'm giving it back. That's Valmiki's homecoming. Not lamps, exactly, but a promise kept on both sides. Rama kept his word to his father; Bharata kept his to Rama. In time, the night Rama came home became one of the stories Diwali tells, especially in North India. Other regions tell other stories for the same night.

663.title: Diwali
663.tomorrow: the later book — Sita's second exile, Lava and Kusha, Sita's return to the earth
663.howItsDone: Traditional Ramayana recitations in temples and homes often end with Rama's coronation, the pattabhishekam, celebrated with a festive meal and the recitation's closing blessing.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Diwali, as Valmiki tells the homecoming. Bharata put the sandals back on his brother's feet. Today, the crowning, and the last page of the war book.

A coronation is a strange kind of party. Everyone dresses up, there are speeches and gifts, and underneath it the whole room asks one question: what will this person do with the power? Valmiki's crowning of Rama has all the glitter: water from the rivers and the seas, priests chanting, the brothers holding the royal umbrella and the fans. But one moment people treasure is small. It happens after the ceremony, between Sita and Hanuman, over a necklace.
screen: `THE CROWNING.` → `RIVERS AND SEAS, POURED OUT.` → `A NECKLACE.`

segments.voice: First, Rama cuts off the matted hair of the forest years and bathes. Then the sacred water is poured over him: the abhisheka, the anointing that makes a king, led by the old family priest Vasishtha. Gifts go out to everyone: priests, friends, the monkey and bear allies who fought beside him. Rama gives Sita a necklace of pearls. And Sita, holding it, keeps looking from the necklace to Hanuman. Rama sees it. Give it to the one you're most pleased with, he tells her. She places it around Hanuman's neck: the one who found her in the ashoka grove when no one else could, and carried her message back. With that, Valmiki brings the war book to its end. Rama, he says, ruled for an enormous span of years, and in his reign no widow mourned, no child died before a parent, the rains came on time. This is where the idea of Rama Rajya comes from, Rama's rule, a picture still used for a just and peaceful order. And the book closes with a promise to whoever hears it: the hearing itself brings blessing. Some traditional readings stop right here. It's a natural ending: the exile over, the promise kept, and, in the festival's version, the lamps all lit. But Valmiki's Ramayana, as it has come down, has one more book. Tomorrow it opens, and it is not a happy one.
screen: `THE ABHISHEKA: A KING ANOINTED.` · `SITA'S PEARLS GO TO HANUMAN.` · `RAMA RAJYA: A PICTURE OF A JUST REIGN.` · `SOME READINGS STOP HERE.` · then, large: `ONE MORE BOOK.`

664.title: the later book — Sita's second exile, Lava and Kusha, Sita's return to the earth
664.hook: the later book — Sita's second exile, Lava and Kusha, Sita's return to the earth
664.tomorrow: the later book — Sita's second exile, Lava and Kusha, Sita's return to the earth
664.howItsDone: Hindu families and teachers handle the Uttara Kanda in different ways: some recite it in full, many traditional readings stop at the coronation, and many retellings tell Sita's exile with open grief and debate.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Diwali, and the crowning. Your line was the pearls go to Hanuman, and the war book closed on a just reign. Today, the book after the ending.

Many recitations of the Ramayana stop at the crowning, with a pearl necklace and a just reign. But the Ramayana as it has come down has one more book. It's called the Uttara Kanda, the later book, or the book that comes after. It gets six days here, and its argument stays open, the way the tradition has left it. Because this book takes the couple who just came home, and pulls them apart again.
screen: `A CROWNING, AND A JUST REIGN.` → `THEN, ONE MORE BOOK.` → `THE COUPLE, PULLED APART AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Uttara means later, or what comes after. Kanda means a section of the poem. This is the seventh book of Valmiki's Ramayana as it has come down. Many scholars think it, and parts of the first book, were added after the core five; others, and many in the tradition, receive all seven as Valmiki's. Both views are held, and there's no settling it here. The book opens with long stories of Ravana's past and Hanuman's childhood, then comes back to Ayodhya. Rama rules; Sita is pregnant; they walk in the palace gardens. One day Rama asks a companion named Bhadra what the people are saying about him. Bhadra hesitates, then tells him. They praise the war, the bridge, the victory. But some say: how can the king take back a wife who lived in Ravana's house? If the king allows it, we'll have to put up with it from our own wives. Rama calls his brothers, tells them what he's heard, and that he has decided. Sita will be taken to the forest near the hermitage of the sage Valmiki, and left there. He forbids them to argue. Once again it falls to Lakshmana to take her, with the charioteer Sumantra at the reins. Sita thinks she's going to visit the hermits, as she had asked. At the Ganga, Lakshmana breaks down, and on the far bank he tells her the truth. The text doesn't make this simple. Rama is shown in grief; Sita is shown blameless. Both are true in the poem, and that is exactly where the argument begins.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Uttara Kanda opened. Gossip reached the king, and Lakshmana left Sita on the bank of the Ganga. Today, two boys are born in a hermitage.

Sita doesn't stay alone on the riverbank for long. Young hermits find her weeping and run to tell their teacher, and he comes down to the water himself. It's Valmiki, the poet, the man who, at the very start of this serial, heard a bird's cry and found the first verse. He takes Sita by the hand and walks her to the women of the hermitage. The poet of the story has just stepped into it.
screen: `THE HERMITS FIND HER.` → `VALMIKI COMES DOWN TO THE WATER.` → `THE POET STEPS INTO THE STORY.`

segments.voice: Valmiki tells Sita he knows who she is and that she's done nothing wrong, and gives her a home among the hermit women. Months later, she gives birth to twins. The Uttara Kanda tells how they got their names. Valmiki prepares protective rites for the newborns with kusha grass, the sacred grass of Vedic ritual. The elder is touched with the tops of the grass, so he is Kusha. The younger with the lower part, the lava, so he is Lava. Then Valmiki does the thing that folds the whole poem back on itself. As the boys grow, he teaches them the Ramayana: not some other song, but this one, with their father as its hero. They learn it by heart and sing it beautifully. Years later, Rama holds a great horse sacrifice, the ashvamedha. Valmiki brings the two boys, and they sing the Ramayana in the open, day after day. Crowds gather. Rama hears it, is moved, and doesn't yet know whose sons are singing. Now, the very first book opens with Kusha and Lava singing the poem before Rama. So that frame was this moment all along. And a week that began in the fire ran through the flight home, Bharata's sandals, the crowning and a second exile, and closes on two boys who don't know they're singing to their own father.
